paras: The threatened lynching of Ed Chamberlain took place at Delphi, Carroll County, Indiana, on the night of April 28, 1888, when rumors spread that a mob from White County would storm the jail holding Chamberlain, who was accused of fatally shooting a young woman at Reynolds. Shortly before midnight the Carroll County sheriff and an armed posse took the prisoner out of the jail and drove him to Lafayette, and no attack was made. A second lynching threat followed in late May at Monticello, after Chamberlain was accused of beating the White County sheriff during a jail escape, and state militia guarded the jail. Chamberlain was never lynched; he hanged himself in jail at Logansport on December 3, 1888, in the middle of his murder trial.

According to the Indianapolis Journal's Delphi correspondent, Chamberlain shot Ella Wattenberg "in a jealous rage" at Reynolds, White County, and she died on the night of April 27. A trial report in November added that the two had known each other since youth, that his love was "unrequited," and that the shooting followed a singing school on the evening of April 17, which she had attended with John Murray, a local telegrapher. The young woman was described as a member of one of the most prominent families in White County, while Chamberlain was said to be rich and his relatives to have "boasted that his money will acquit him," which the Journal said gave color to the mob rumors. Delphi had seen a lynching seven months earlier, when Amer Green was taken from the same jail, and the correspondent tied the town's excitement to that memory.

After the young woman died, feeling ran so high that Chamberlain was taken from jail at midnight and moved to Delphi. On the night of April 28 the streets were crowded, the jail was guarded, and Sheriff Nelson Van Gundy declared that under no circumstance would he surrender the prisoner. A judge had already ordered Chamberlain sent to the penitentiary at Michigan City the next day if no assault came. Instead, about an hour before midnight, the sheriff and an armed posse "quietly spirited the prisoner out of the rear of the jail" and drove by closed carriage to Lafayette, arriving shortly after midnight. The correspondent wrote that the authorities had "positive information" of an assault by "an indignant organization from White county," while a Lafayette dispatch quoted Chamberlain as saying he did not fear a mob.

Within days his father, Henry Chamberlain, told reporters in Lafayette that there was no danger of mob violence even in Reynolds. On May 3 White County Sheriff Henderson took the prisoner back to Monticello, saying he expected no trouble from a mob though feeling against Chamberlain was strong.

On the night of May 24, according to a Monticello dispatch, Chamberlain and two tramps held for highway robbery, Robert Catterson and Albert Benson, attacked Sheriff Henderson with an iron bar as he locked them in and escaped. Neighbors led by Jacob Fisher, tipped off by his cousin Mary Biddle, found Chamberlain asleep at his uncle William Biddle's house and brought him bound to the Monticello jail early on May 26. Crowds came in by train and road, and a dispatch printed in the Maysville Evening Bulletin said "the general opinion is that he will be hung by a mob." At Judge Gould's request Governor Gray sent a militia company from Delphi under Captain Edward Gresham, which took over the jail from the civil officers.

The Indiana State Sentinel's correspondent counted about 1,500 people in town that night and said a reported band of 100 men west of town proved to be about fifty who "lacked organization" and dispersed. A Wabash dispatch in the New-York Tribune described instead "a band of four hundred armed lynchers" from Reynolds who halted on the outskirts, deterred by the militia. Neither account reported an attack on the jail.

Benson, recaptured, was sentenced on May 26 to five years in the northern prison. No arrests of anyone in the threatened mobs appear in the coverage. Chamberlain's murder trial opened at Logansport on November 28, with a jury drawn from a venire of fifty-two men and insanity as the defense. On the morning of December 3 he hanged himself in jail with a strip of bed ticking, and jurors later said the evidence had been overwhelming.

The story began as a special to the Indianapolis Journal headed "LYNCHING THREATENED," and its wire version ran within two days in the Wichita Eagle as "A Lynching Feared," in the New York Sun as "In Danger of Lynching," and in the Louisville Weekly Courier-Journal as "Saved from a Mob." The Journal repeated its midnight dispatch the next day, and brief items in the Indiana State Sentinel and the Maysville Evening Bulletin compressed the case to the death and the threat: "Citizens threatened to lynch the murderer." Papers called Chamberlain "the murderer" from the first day, long before any trial.

The May escape drew wider coverage, and some papers treated a lynching as likely: the Somerset Herald wrote that he "will surely be lynched if caught." The New-York Tribune called him a "worthless fellow" of "deficient intellect" and spoke of "Judge Lynch's court," while crediting the militia's rifles with turning the mob back. The Sentinel's Monticello correspondent, by contrast, reported that Judge Gould was censured for a "premature" call for troops. When the case ended, the St. Paul Daily Globe headlined the suicide "CHOSE TO HANG HIMSELF" and said he had saved the county "the Expense of an Execution." None of the reports mentions the race of anyone involved.

The young woman's name appears as Ella Wattenberg, Ida Wittenberg, Etta Wittenburg and Ida M. Wittenburg, and the Wichita Eagle's copy called the accused "Fred" Chamberlain. The first dispatch placed the shooting "one week ago" on April 28, while the later and fuller trial report dated it April 17. The Somerset Herald headlined its escape story "They Killed the Sheriff," but other May reports said only that Henderson's life was despaired of, and no report of his death appears in the coverage.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Ed Chamberlain
bases: Papers reported a mob organized in White county to take Chamberlain from the Delphi jail and lynch him, averted when the sheriff removed him (A1, A2), with a second lynching threat at Monticello in May (A14, A16); no one was killed by a mob.

A group reported to be organizing to take an accused murderer from jail and lynch him would have acted illegally under a pretext of justice (A1, A2, A14), but no attack was made and Chamberlain later died by his own hand in jail (A18); this was a threatened lynching only.

The Delphi correspondent and a separate Lafayette dispatch both report the removal for fear of a mob (A2), and later Lafayette and Logansport reports confirm he was taken to Lafayette for safekeeping (A10, A17); the father's denial of danger (A9) comes from an interested party after the fact.

accounts.label: Delphi correspondent (Indianapolis Journal)
accounts.gist: A White county mob was organized to storm the jail; the sheriff vowed not to surrender the prisoner and, on 'positive information' of an assault, removed him at midnight.

accounts.label: Accused's father
accounts.gist: Henry Chamberlain said there was no danger of mob violence even in Reynolds and the people were willing to let the law take its course.

accounts.label: White County sheriff
accounts.gist: Sheriff Henderson expected no trouble from a mob on returning the prisoner to Monticello, though feeling against him was strong.

accounts.label: Monticello correspondent (Indiana State Sentinel)
accounts.gist: After the recapture, threats of lynching grew once militia arrived; a reported band of 100 proved to be about fifty disorganized men who dispersed.

accounts.label: Wabash dispatch (New-York Tribune)
accounts.gist: Four hundred armed lynchers from Reynolds halted outside Monticello, deterred by the militia's rifles.

framing.detail: The Journal's 'LYNCHING THREATENED' report treated the mob as a danger the sheriff had to avert, while noting the prisoner's wealth gave 'color' to the rumors and calling him 'the murderer'.
Out-of-state papers ran the Delphi dispatch under 'A LYNCHING FEARED', 'In Danger of Lynching' and 'SAVED FROM A MOB'.
The New-York Tribune scorned the 'worthless fellow' and his 'deficient intellect' and spoke of 'Judge Lynch's court', while crediting the militia with deterring the mob.
The Somerset Herald predicted he 'will surely be lynched if caught', reporting it as expectation rather than condemning it.
The St. Paul Globe headlined the suicide 'CHOSE TO HANG HIMSELF' and said he saved the expense of an execution.
